6.1.summary: The universe isn't out to get you. The stuff everything is made of simply goes where it's shaped, and the reason that shapes it, the intelligence Marcus sees running through nature, has no malice in it. It does no wrong and harms nothing. Everything that comes into being and comes to an end happens by that same orderly reason, so there's no hidden cruelty to resent.

6.2.summary:
When you're doing what you should, the conditions don't matter much: whether you're cold or warm, tired or rested, criticised or praised. Marcus even adds dying to the list. Death is just one more thing we do in life, and like everything else, the task is simply to do it well when it comes.

The idea is to keep your attention on the job in front of you rather than on how comfortable or admired you feel while doing it.
6.2.today: Think of finishing the report when you're short on sleep, looking after a sick child on a freezing morning, or carrying on with a project after someone has rubbished it online. The tiredness and the criticism are real, but they don't change what doing the work well looks like.

6.3.summary: Look beneath the surface. With anything you meet, notice what it actually is and what it's really worth, instead of taking its appearance or its reputation on trust. Marcus is reminding himself not to let either of those slip past unexamined.

6.4.summary: Everything that exists will soon change. Either it will be turned into vapour, if all matter is ultimately one substance, or it will be scattered into its separate atoms. Marcus doesn't mind which theory is right. On either view, nothing you see around you is going to last.

6.5.summary: Your mind, the part of you that reasons and directs everything else, can know itself. It understands what state it's in, what it's doing, and what material it's working with. That self-awareness is what lets you take charge of your own judgements instead of being pushed around by them.

6.6.summary: The best revenge is not to become like the person who wronged you. Hitting back in kind just means they've changed you for the worse. Staying decent is the one response that leaves you better off than they are.
6.6.today: When someone sends a snide email, the satisfying reply is usually an even snider one. Not sending it, and staying the kind of person who wouldn't, is the version of getting even that doesn't cost you anything.

6.7.summary: Find your joy and your rest in one simple thing: moving from one good act for others to the next, with God, or the order of the universe, in mind. Marcus is suggesting that a life of steady service, done with a sense of something larger, can be enough by itself.
6.7.today: That might mean going from helping a colleague with a problem, to cooking dinner for the family, to ringing a friend who's having a hard time, and finding satisfaction in the chain of small useful acts rather than in waiting for the weekend.

6.8.summary: Your mind sets itself in motion and decides what kind of mind it will be. And in doing that, it also decides how everything that happens looks to it. Events arrive, but the meaning they have for you is shaped by your own judgement. That is both a responsibility and a freedom.

6.9.summary: Everything that happens happens according to the nature of the universe, the single way the whole world works. There is no rival nature, whether outside the world, hidden inside it, or separate from it, that could be making things happen instead. Marcus is reminding himself that there is one order to things, and everything belongs to it.

6.10.summary:
Marcus runs through the familiar choice: either the universe is a random tangle of atoms, or it is unified, ordered and guided by a purpose. If it's random, why would he want to hang around in such a mess, and why worry, since he'll come apart into dust whatever he does? If it's ordered, he can feel reverence, stand firm, and trust whatever governs it.

Either way, anxiety makes no sense. Both possibilities lead him back to calm.

6.11.summary: Circumstances will sometimes knock you off balance. That's unavoidable. The skill is to come back to yourself quickly and not stay out of tune for longer than the disruption lasts. Like a musician who keeps returning to the right note, the more often you come back to your own steadiness, the better you get at holding it.
6.11.today: After a tense phone call or a row at home, you'll be rattled for a bit. The practice is to notice it and return to your normal self as soon as the moment passes, rather than replaying it on the drive home or carrying it into the evening.

6.12.summary:
Marcus compares his life at the imperial court to a stepmother and philosophy to a mother. You'd treat a stepmother respectfully, but you'd keep going back to your real mother. So he should do his duties at court, but keep returning to philosophy and resting in it.

It's philosophy that makes court life bearable for him, and that makes him bearable to the people at court.
6.12.today: Your job, or a demanding caring role, might be the stepmother. The mother is whatever restores you and keeps you decent: reading, a walk, quiet reflection. Going back to it often is what lets you handle the rest without becoming difficult yourself.

6.13.summary:
Strip things down to what they really are. Fine food is the dead body of a fish, bird or pig; Falernian, a prized Roman wine, is fermented grape juice; a purple imperial robe is sheep's wool dyed with shellfish blood. Seeing things this plainly cuts through their glamour.

Marcus wants to do this with everything that seems impressive, peeling away the grand language around it. Outward show distorts our reasoning most when we're surest we're busy with something important. He ends with a nod to something the Cynic philosopher Crates said about Xenocrates, a head of Plato's school, presumably deflating his dignity.
6.13.today: A designer handbag is leather and stitching. A job title is a few words on a business card. The car you're tempted to stretch for is metal, glass and a loan. Describing things this flatly can take the heat out of wanting them.

6.14.summary:
Marcus ranks what people admire. Most people admire things that merely hold together, like stones, timber, vines and olive groves. Slightly wiser people admire living things like flocks and herds. Better-educated people admire minds, but only clever or skilled ones, or simply owning many slaves.

The person who truly values a reasoning mind, one that sees itself as part of the whole human community, cares about nothing else. They keep their own mind working in line with reason and the common good, and they work alongside others who share that aim.
6.14.today: Today's version might be admiring property, then pets and horses, then talented people you can hire or show off. The deeper thing to value is your own mind and character, used for others, not a collection of impressive possessions or people.

6.15.summary:
Everything is in a rush, some things coming into being and others passing away, and even what's arriving is partly gone already. The world is renewed by constant change, like the endless flow of time. In a river like that, what would you set your heart on? It would be like falling in love with a sparrow that's already flown out of sight.

Your own life is like this too. Just as you take in a breath and give it back, you'll one day give back the whole power of breathing you received at birth, which was really only yesterday.

6.16.summary:
What's actually worth valuing? Not the things we share with plants and animals, like breathing, eating, reacting to impressions or being jerked about by desires. Not applause either, or the clapping of tongues that is public praise. What's left is acting and holding back in line with your own nature, which is what every craft and all education aim at.

If you value other things, you'll never be free or content. You'll be envious and suspicious of anyone who might take them, and you'll resent the gods. Respecting your own mind makes you content with yourself, at ease with others, and accepting of how things are.
6.16.today: If your sense of worth rides on follower counts, a promotion or someone else's approval, you'll feel threatened by every rival and every bad review. Valuing how well you think and act is something nobody can take away, which is why it brings peace.

6.17.summary: The elements swirl all around us, above and below. But virtue doesn't move like they do. Its progress is something more divine: it travels a path that is barely noticed, and it goes happily on its way. Being good rarely looks dramatic from the outside.

6.18.summary: People are strange. They won't praise the people living right alongside them, yet they badly want praise from future generations they'll never meet. Marcus points out how absurd that is: it's about as sensible as being upset that people who lived before you didn't praise you.
6.18.today: Think of people who chase a legacy or imagine how they'll be remembered, while barely thanking the colleague at the next desk or the partner who cooks most nights. The appreciation that's actually possible is the kind you give and get now.

6.19.summary: If something is hard for you, don't assume it's impossible for anyone. And if something is possible for human beings and suits our nature, assume you can do it too. Other people's achievements are evidence of what you are capable of.
6.19.today: If a colleague learnt a new language at forty, or a neighbour gave up smoking, or a friend ran their first 10k after years off, that's proof the thing can be done by an ordinary person. The difficulty you feel isn't the same as impossibility.

6.20.summary:
In a training bout, if someone scratches you or butts your head, you don't take it personally, sulk, or decide they're treacherous. You just keep an eye on them and step out of the way, without hostility. Marcus wants to treat the rest of life like that.

Many people who knock into you are more like sparring partners than enemies. You can overlook a lot, avoid getting hurt again, and still feel neither suspicion nor hatred.
6.20.today: In five-a-side football someone clips your ankle and you shrug it off. Do the same with the driver who cuts you up or the colleague who talks over you: give them a bit more room next time, but don't build a grudge out of it.

6.21.summary: If someone can show Marcus he's thinking or acting wrongly, he'll gladly change. He's after the truth, and the truth never harmed anyone. What harms you is clinging to a mistake out of pride or ignorance. Being corrected is a gift, not a defeat.
6.21.today: When someone points out an error in your spreadsheet, or a friend says you were unfair in an argument, the instinct is to defend yourself. Saying 'you're right, thanks' costs a moment's pride and leaves you better off.

6.22.summary: Marcus does his duty and doesn't let other things trouble him. Whatever else there is falls into three groups: things without life, creatures without reason, or people who have lost their way and don't know the right road. None of these is a reason to be thrown off his own work.

6.23.summary: Treat animals and things, which have no reason, generously and freely, since you have reason and they don't. Treat human beings, who share reason with you, as fellow members of a community. And keep turning to the gods throughout, without fretting about how long you'll get to do this. Even three hours lived this way would be enough.
6.23.today: That might look like being careful with a borrowed car or kind to the dog, while giving people something more: patience with the slow cashier, real attention to the friend who calls. A short life lived like that isn't a lesser one.

6.24.summary: Alexander the Great and the man who looked after his horses ended up in exactly the same condition. Either both were taken back into the creative source of the universe, or both were scattered into atoms. Whatever death is, it treats the conqueror and the stable hand alike.

6.25.summary: Think how many things happen inside you at a single instant, in your body and your mind together. Once you see that, it's no longer surprising that far more, indeed everything that exists, can be happening at once in the single whole we call the universe. Marcus is stretching his sense of scale to make the cosmos feel less bewildering.

6.26.summary:
If someone asked you how to spell your name, you wouldn't shout each letter at them. And if they got angry, you wouldn't get angry back. You'd just calmly go through it, letter by letter. Marcus uses his own name, Antoninus, as the example.

Every duty is made up of steps like that. Your job is to work through them one at a time, without getting rattled or matching the anger of people who are cross with you, until the task is done.
6.26.today: When a customer on the phone is furious, or a child is shouting about homework, the temptation is to raise your voice too. Going through the steps patiently, one at a time, gets it finished faster and leaves you calmer.

6.27.summary: People do wrong because they're chasing what they believe is good for them. They're mistaken, but that's their motive. So when you're angry at them, you're in a sense denying them the right to pursue what they think will help them, which is harsh. Better to teach them and show them the truth, without anger.
6.27.today: The teenager who lies to get out of trouble, or the colleague who cuts a corner, thinks they're doing the sensible thing. Explaining calmly why it isn't will do more good than an outburst.

6.28.summary: Death is the end of the senses pulling at you, of desires jerking you around like strings on a puppet, of thoughts wandering off in all directions, and of having to look after the body. Marcus describes it as a kind of rest from all the things that keep a person busy and unsettled, without fear or drama.

6.29.summary: It's shameful for your mind and spirit to give up while your body is still going strong. If you can still walk, work and breathe, then giving in inwardly, losing your nerve or your standards, is the real failure.

6.30.summary:
Marcus warns himself not to be turned into a typical Caesar, soaked in the colour of power the way cloth takes a dye. He lists what he wants to stay instead: simple, good, sincere, serious, unpretentious, just, devout, kind and hard-working. Life is short, and its only real harvest is a reverent attitude and acts that help others.

His model is Antoninus Pius, his adoptive father and the emperor before him: steady, unhurried, careful to understand things, deaf to gossip, content with little, patient with critics and glad to be corrected. Marcus wants to copy him so he can die with as clear a conscience.
6.30.today: Anyone given power, whether as a manager, a team captain or the person running the family group chat, can get dyed by it. The antidote is to pick a real person you admire, and ask how they would handle the meeting, the complaint or the credit for a success.

6.31.summary: Wake up and come to your senses. When you wake from a nightmare, you realise it was only a dream that upset you. Marcus wants to look at the troubles of waking life the same way, as things that seem frightening but have no real hold on him once seen clearly.
6.31.today: The worry that kept you up at 3am, about an email or an awkward conversation, often looks small over breakfast. The trick is to bring that morning view to the things that are bothering you right now.

6.32.summary: Marcus is made of a body and a mind. To the body, everything is the same; it can't judge one thing better than another. To the mind, the only things that matter are its own actions, because those are in its power. And even then, only its present actions count. What it did in the past or will do later can't be acted on now, so for the moment they don't matter either.

6.33.summary: Hands and feet don't suffer from doing their own work, as long as each does its proper job. In the same way, hard work is not unnatural for a person, so long as it's the kind of work a human being is meant to do. And if it suits your nature, it can't be bad for you.
6.33.today: Long hours on a project you believe in, helping a friend move house, or nursing a parent can be exhausting. Marcus would say tiredness from doing your proper work isn't harm, even if it doesn't feel pleasant.

6.34.summary: Robbers, murderers of their own parents and tyrants have all enjoyed plenty of pleasures. Marcus's point in this one blunt line is that pleasure can't be what makes life good, because the worst people have had as much of it as anyone.

6.35.summary: Skilled craftspeople will go along with untrained clients up to a point, but they won't abandon the core principles of their trade. Architects and doctors stick to their rules. So isn't it strange if a person has less respect for their own reason, the thing they share with the gods, than a builder has for building?
6.35.today: A good plumber will listen to what you want but won't fit the pipe in a way that will leak. Yet people will drop their own principles to please the room in a meeting or keep the peace at dinner. Your reason deserves at least as much loyalty as a tradesperson's standards.

6.36.summary:
Asia and Europe are mere corners of the universe, the sea a drop, Mount Athos a clod of earth, all present time a pinprick in eternity. Everything is small, changeable and short-lived, and it all flows from the same source that governs the whole.

Even the lion's jaws, poison, thorns and mud are by-products of something grand and beautiful. Don't think they come from a different source than the things you revere. Form a fair view of the whole, rough edges included.

6.37.summary: If you've really seen what is happening now, you've seen everything that ever happened and everything that ever will. All things are of one kind and follow the same patterns. History may change its costumes, but human life and nature play out in much the same way.

6.38.summary: Think often about how everything in the universe is connected and related. In a sense, all things are woven together and are therefore friendly to each other. One thing follows another in order, because the whole world moves together as a single, unified substance working in concert.

6.39.summary: Fit yourself to the circumstances you've been given, and love the people you've ended up living among, and mean it. Marcus isn't asking for tolerance or politeness, but for real affection towards the people fate has placed around you.
6.39.today: You didn't pick your colleagues, your in-laws or the neighbours on your street. Making the best of the job you're in, and actually caring about those people rather than wishing for different ones, is what Marcus means.

6.40.summary: A tool or a pot works well when it does its job, even though its maker has long since left. But in living things, the power that made them stays inside them. That makes it even more fitting to respect that power, and to see that if you live in line with it, everything in you is in keeping with intelligence, just as everything in the universe is.

6.41.summary:
If you think things outside your control, like money, health or reputation, are truly good or bad for you, then when you lose them you'll blame the gods and hate whoever caused it, or whoever you suspect might have. Much of the wrong we do comes from not treating these things as indifferent.

If you count only your own choices as good or bad, there's nothing left to blame the gods for and no reason to turn on other people.
6.41.today: If you see a promotion as your whole worth, the colleague who got it becomes an enemy and the boss a villain. If what matters is how you do your work and treat people, losing out stings but doesn't turn you bitter.

6.42.summary:
Everyone is working towards one end, some knowingly and some without realising it, like sleepers whom Heraclitus, the early Greek philosopher, called fellow-workers in what happens in the world. Even the people who complain about events and try to resist them play a part; the universe has a use for them too.

So the question is what kind of worker you choose to be. You'll be put to use either way. Marcus just doesn't want to be like the silly line in a comedy that Chrysippus, the great Stoic thinker, mentioned: something worthless in itself that the play happens to include.

6.43.summary: Everything in nature has its own job. The sun doesn't try to be rain, and the stars all differ, yet together they make one working whole. People are the same: you don't have to do everyone's part, only your own, and do it well, trusting that different roles add up to something shared.

6.44.summary:
Marcus works through the possibilities. If the gods have planned his life, they've planned it well, since they have no reason to wish him harm. If they've only planned the whole, then what happens to him follows from that, and he should accept it gladly. If they plan nothing at all, which he thinks it wrong to believe, he can still decide for himself what is useful.

And what's useful is what suits his nature, which is rational and social. As emperor his city is Rome, but as a human being it is the whole world. Only what benefits those communities benefits him.

6.45.summary: Whatever happens to each person serves the good of the whole, and that alone should be enough. But you'll also notice that what genuinely benefits one person tends to benefit others too. Marcus adds a careful note: here he means 'benefit' in the everyday sense, things like money or health, which Stoics count as neither good nor bad in themselves.

6.46.summary: At the games in the amphitheatre, seeing the same spectacles over and over becomes tiresome. Life as a whole is the same, Marcus says, because everything everywhere is the same stuff repeating. He ends with a weary question, 'How long, then?', as if wondering how long he'll be watching the same show.
6.46.today: It's the feeling of scrolling through the same kinds of headlines, rows and viral clips for the hundredth time and realising nothing is really new. Marcus treats that weariness as an honest observation rather than something to fix.

6.47.summary:
Keep in mind that people of every kind, every job and every nation have died, down to the obscure names nobody remembers. Then think of the great ones: philosophers like Heraclitus, Pythagoras and Socrates, heroes, generals and tyrants, brilliant minds like Eudoxus, Hipparchus and Archimedes, and the Cynic satirist Menippus who mocked human life itself. All of them have long been dust.

What harm is that to them, or to the forgotten? Only one thing here is worth much: to live truthfully and justly, and to be kind even to liars and wrongdoers.

6.48.summary: When you need cheering up, think about the good qualities of the people around you: one person's energy, another's modesty, another's generosity. Nothing lifts the spirits like seeing virtues living in the people you share your days with, so keep those examples close at hand.
6.48.today: On a grim day, try listing what you admire in the people near you: the colleague who always makes the tea, the friend who never gossips, the partner who stays patient with the kids. It's a better pick-me-up than another scroll through your phone.

6.49.summary: You don't resent weighing only so many pounds rather than three hundred. So why resent having only so many years rather than more? Just as you accept the size of body you were given, accept the length of life you were given. A litra was a Roman measure of weight, roughly a pound.

6.50.summary:
Try to persuade people, but act even without their agreement when justice demands it. If someone blocks you by force, accept it calmly and use the obstacle to practise a different virtue, like patience. Remember that you always aimed with a reservation, never expecting to do the impossible.

So what did you actually want? To make the right effort. And you've done that, even if the outcome didn't happen.
6.50.today: You argued for a change at work and were overruled. You did the part that was yours, which was making the case well. Now the task is accepting the decision gracefully, and perhaps showing patience with the people who disagreed.

6.51.summary: Someone who loves fame places their good in other people's actions, in what others say and do about them. Someone who loves pleasure places it in their own sensations. A person with understanding places their good in their own actions, the one thing actually in their hands.
6.51.today: If your day is made or ruined by how many people liked your post, your happiness is in strangers' thumbs. If it depends on the next meal or drink, it's in your stomach. Measuring the day by how well you acted keeps it in your own hands.

6.52.summary: You can decline to form an opinion about something, and so stay undisturbed. Things themselves don't have the power to make you judge them one way or another. The judgement is yours, which means the disturbance is optional.

6.53.summary: Make a habit of listening closely to what other people say, and as far as you can, getting inside their heads to understand what they really mean and why they're saying it.
6.53.today: In a meeting, that might mean actually hearing the objection instead of planning your reply. In a disagreement at home, it might mean asking what's really bothering the other person before you defend yourself.

6.54.summary: What isn't good for the hive isn't good for the bee either. You can't really gain from something that harms the community you belong to, because your good and the common good are bound together.

6.55.summary: If sailors hurled abuse at the helmsman, or patients at their doctor, who else would they listen to? And how could the helmsman keep the ship safe, or the doctor cure the sick? Marcus seems to be thinking about leadership: people need to trust and listen to those charged with looking after them, or no one can help them.

6.56.summary: How many of the people who came into the world when Marcus did have already left it. A short, plain reminder that death isn't a distant event but something already happening all around his own generation.

6.57.summary: To someone with jaundice, honey tastes bitter; to someone with rabies, water is frightening; to small children a ball is a treasure. So why get angry at people? A false belief distorts how someone sees things just as powerfully as illness does. They aren't choosing to see wrongly any more than a sick person chooses bitterness.
6.57.today: When a friend who's been badly hurt reads every message as a slight, or someone deep in a conspiracy theory dismisses everything you say, anger won't help. They're seeing through a kind of fever, and patience makes more sense.

6.58.summary: No one can stop you living by your own reason, and nothing will happen to you that goes against the reason of the universe. Your character is always yours to direct, and whatever comes your way is part of the order of things. Between those two facts, there's nothing left to fear.

6.59.summary: Think about the kind of people we try to impress, what we hope to gain from them, and what we do to win their approval. Then think how quickly time will bury all of it, and how much it has buried already. Seen this way, chasing people's good opinion looks a poor use of a life.
6.59.today: Consider who you're really dressing for, posting for or staying late to impress, and what you'd actually get. In a few years most of those people won't remember, and the moment will be long gone.
